summary: Elizabeth Lopatto's trial report for The Verge covers Sam Bankman-Fried's direct testimony in his fraud trial. She argues he undermined his own credibility with claims about Alameda Research's name, the "allow_negative" feature, the lack of a risk team, and what he knew about the roughly $8 billion Alameda owed FTX, which contradict earlier trial evidence the jury had seen. The piece also notes the judge scolding him for not answering questions.
one_line: The Verge recounts Sam Bankman-Fried's direct testimony at his fraud trial, highlighting claims about Alameda and FTX that conflicted with evidence the jury had already seen.
key_facts: Judge Lewis Kaplan scolded Sam Bankman-Fried for not answering questions from his own counsel Mark Cohen on direct examination; the day before he was scolded for not answering prosecutor Danielle Sassoon's cross-examination questions at an evidentiary hearing.
Three times during direct testimony, an "Objection, narrative!" to Bankman-Fried's answers was sustained.

Bankman-Fried started Alameda Research in 2017 during a crypto bull run, saying he knew "basically nothing" about cryptocurrency but wanted to do arbitrage; it was named for Alameda County, California, where its first office was set up.

Bankman-Fried testified the name was meant to keep the firm under the radar and that the internal name had been Wireless Mouse; Lopatto notes a podcast video, shown during Gary Wang's testimony, had him saying the name made it easier to get a bank account.
He hired Gary Wang, then Nishad Singh about a month after founding Alameda, then Caroline Ellison, and claimed he did not supervise Wang's direct work.

He testified arbitrage returned 50 to 100 percent annualized and that he gave FTX only a 20 percent chance of success; he said he handled support tickets "periodically" but called not creating a risk team a "big mistake."

Bankman-Fried testified the FTX risk engine was "sagging under the weight" of growth in 2020 and got stuck in a feedback loop that could have caused losses in the "trillions of dollars," and he said this led to "allow_negative," which he claimed not to know about until recently.
Lopatto says "allow_negative" was coded and switched on in 2019, and that she, Bankman-Fried and the jury saw the code in court.

In 2021 FTX had $1 billion of revenue; Bankman-Fried said he worked 12 to 22 hours a day and handed Alameda to Caroline Ellison and Sam Trabucco as co-CEOs, while denying he knew Singh backdated interest payments to reach $1 billion.
Bankman-Fried said Alameda took the MobileCoin loss because he thought it appropriate for it to act as a backstop liquidity provider.

In June 2022 he heard of the "fiat@ftx" account tracking what Alameda owed FTX but did not investigate, and he directed Ellison to repay Alameda's lenders; he also gave capital infusions to BlockFi and Voyager.
Bankman-Fried said he did not learn of the $8 billion Alameda liability until October 2022, by looking at a computer database, and was "very surprised!"
He disputed Adam Yedidia's August 2022 account and said the balcony conversation with Singh was about Alameda's liabilities and FTX marketing spending, not money owed to FTX.
The article notes Bankman-Fried has been found guilty on seven counts including wire fraud, and the SEC alleged FTX was a fraud "from the start."
